q: Name a cipher or public-key algorithm.

answers.l: Rijndael, by Daemen and Rijmen. Won NIST’s open competition in 2000.
Rivest, Shamir and Adleman, 1977. Clifford Cocks at GCHQ found it in 1973, classified until 1997.
1977, from IBM’s Lucifer with a 56-bit key. Publicly cracked in about 22 hours in 1999.
1976. Two parties agree on a secret over a public channel.
Shift each letter by three. Suetonius says Caesar used it.
A Caesar shift of 13, so encrypting twice decrypts.
Called "le chiffre indéchiffrable" for three centuries until Babbage and Kasiski broke it.
Perfect secrecy, if the key is truly random, as long as the message, and never reused.
DES three times, for a longer effective key.
Ron Rivest, 1987. Leaked in 1994. Its weaknesses broke WEP.
Bruce Schneier, 1993. Unpatented on purpose.
Daniel J. Bernstein. Fast in software, with no lookup tables to leak timing.
In 2010, Sony’s PS3 reused an ECDSA nonce, exposing its private signing key.
Bernstein and colleagues. Deterministic nonces, so no PS3-style mistakes.
A rotor machine broken first by Polish cryptanalysts, then at Bletchley Park.
Schneier’s AES finalist.
Anderson, Biham and Knudsen. The AES runner-up, with a bigger safety margin.
Bernstein, 2005. The elliptic curve behind X25519 key exchange.
ChaCha’s predecessor and an eSTREAM winner.
NIST, 1991. Dropped for new signatures in FIPS 186-5, 2023.
Taher Elgamal, 1985. He later led SSL’s development at Netscape.
ML-KEM, standardized by NIST in 2024. Post-quantum key exchange already shipping in browsers.
Charles Wheatstone invented it. Lord Playfair promoted it.
Mitsubishi and NTT, 2000. Japan’s answer to AES.
Used in early PGP.
Rivest, 1994. Data-dependent rotations.
The NSA cipher inside the Clipper chip. Declassified in 1998.
A random number generator with a suspected NSA backdoor. RSA Security reportedly took $10 million to make it the default.
ML-DSA, NIST’s main post-quantum signature standard, 2024.
Lattice-based, 1996. Post-quantum before it was cool.
Tiny Encryption Algorithm, Wheeler and Needham, 1994. A few lines of C.
TEA with its key schedule weaknesses fixed.
The GSM phone cipher, broken in practice.
A post-quantum candidate broken in 2022 in about an hour on a single core.
IBM’s predecessor to DES, by Horst Feistel.
Schneier’s cipher for a deck of playing cards, written for Cryptonomicon.
The tweakable block cipher inside Skein.
An NSA lightweight cipher. ISO declined to standardize it in 2018.
Simon’s sibling. Also declined by ISO in 2018.
An AES finalist.
IBM’s AES finalist.
China’s national block cipher.
Russia’s GOST block cipher. The name means grasshopper.
Additively homomorphic: multiply ciphertexts, get the encrypted sum.
1978, built on error-correcting codes. Huge keys, still unbroken.
Hash-based post-quantum signatures, standardized as SLH-DSA.
Michael Rabin, 1979. Provably as hard as factoring.
A 1978 public-key scheme. Shamir broke it in 1982.
A strip of leather wound around a rod. A Spartan transposition cipher.
Reverse the alphabet. It appears in the Hebrew Bible.
Japan’s WWII diplomatic cipher machine, broken by the US Army’s Signal Intelligence Service.
The German high command’s teleprinter cipher. Colossus was built to break it.

nope.base64: An encoding. Not encryption, whatever the ticket says.
nope.sha256: A hash. Try the hash drill.
nope.md5: A hash, and a broken one.
nope.xor: An operation. The one-time pad is the cipher.
nope.tls: A protocol that uses several of these.
nope.ssl: A protocol that uses several of these.
nope.pgp: A system built from several of these.
